summary: Defines a MIB module with textual conventions for the IPv6 Flow Label. Other MIB modules can import it instead of defining their own versions. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: The flow label is a small tag in IPv6 messages. This memo defines one shared way to describe it for management tools.

questions: what is the ipv6 flow label mib
what is a textual convention in a mib
what range can an ipv6 flow label have
subtitle: Two shared MIB data types so every management module describes the IPv6 Flow Label the same way.

tldr.problem: Several MIB modules defined their own, different objects for the IPv6 Flow Label, which caused confusion and unnecessary complexity.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3595 defines two textual conventions, IPv6FlowLabel and IPv6FlowLabelOrAny, in the IPV6-FLOW-LABEL-MIB module for other MIB modules to import.
tldr.outcome: Management modules can now represent a flow label one way, including a -1 wildcard for 'any value'. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3595 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Several standards-track MIB modules had defined objects to represent an IPv6 Flow Label (sometimes called Flow ID), as well as IPv6 Flow Label filters. The flow label is a field in the IPv6 packet header, specified in RFC 2460. The result of this was a set of different definitions for the same piece of management information, which the RFC says may lead to confusion and unnecessary complexity.

This document defines a set of textual conventions (TCs) that can and should be reused in MIB modules, so they all represent an IPv6 Flow Label in the same way. PIB modules can and should also use these TCs when they need to represent a flow label.
sections.eli5: Many people wrote down the same label in different ways. This memo picks one way so everyone can match.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content:
The RFC sits inside the Internet-Standard Management Framework, which is described in section 7 of RFC 3410. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), generally using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

Objects in a MIB are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant with SMIv2, which is described in STD 58: RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.eli5: Network gear keeps a big shared notebook of facts about itself. The notebook has strict rules for how to write things in it, and this memo follows them.

sections.title: The Two Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module IPV6-FLOW-LABEL-MIB defines two textual conventions, both with the display hint d (plain decimal) and status current. Both are based on Integer32.

  • IPv6FlowLabel is the flow identifier in an IPv6 packet header that may be used to discriminate traffic flows. Its range is 0..1048575. Its REFERENCE points to section 6 of the IPv6 specification, RFC 2460.
  • IPv6FlowLabelOrAny has the same meaning, but the value -1 is used to indicate a wildcard, that is, any value. Its range is -1 | 0..1048575.

The second form was added because 3GPP expressed a requirement to be able to specify a wildcard for a flow ID or flow label, as noted in the acknowledgments.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of label box. One holds a number from zero up to a big limit. The other can also say 'any label at all' by holding minus one.

sections.title: The Module Definition
sections.content:
The module is registered as ipv6FlowLabelMIB with { mib-2 103 }. It imports MODULE-IDENTITY, mib-2 and Integer32 from SNMPv2-SMI, and TEXTUAL-CONVENTION from SNMPv2-TC. Its organization is the IETF Operations and Management Area, and its editor is Bert Wijnen.

The module has a single revision, dated 28 August 2003, described as the initial version published as RFC 3595. The module defines no management objects of its own; it only defines types for other modules to use.
sections.eli5: The memo includes the official form that computers read. It has a name tag, a date, and the two label types, and nothing else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB module defines no management objects. It defines only textual conventions that other MIB modules may use to define objects.

The RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written for MIB modules that define concrete management objects. It therefore concludes that this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: This memo only makes a label type and does not do anything on its own, so it cannot cause a security problem by itself.
